    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    • Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial new terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media manufacturer declared today.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial new terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media manufacturer declared today.

    It has been revealed that “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms enhancement. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms. Until then our existing terms remain in place.”.

    Meta did not answer Nieman Lab’s questions about which news industry groups and leaders Meta intends to consult.

    According to recent reports, the proposed terms have drawn criticism because they would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and potentially allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models, with no option to opt out. Last week, Meta unveiled it would push back implementation of its new terms to November 20 in order to “explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab. Meta had previously revised its new terms to remove the word “train.” No version of the terms has included language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

    Shortly after Stone’s announcement, a Norwegian court blocked Meta’s terms from taking effect on November 20 until the court had assessed their legality, the country’s public broadcaster NRK reported.

    It has been revealed that “We are satisfied that the court has agreed with us that Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the latest terms are unreasonable,” said Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, MBL’s board chair, in a news release. “We are also pleased that the court recognizes that the alternative is that media companies risk losing control over editorial content built up over many years.”.

    In a recent development, since Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15, publishers and politicians around the world have pushed back, filing complaints with national competition authorities, calling on the European Commission to investigate, and writing letters to Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Two United States senators — California Democrat Adam Schiff and Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn — each separately wrote to Zuckerberg, insisting that the manufacturer withdraw the terms as they’re right now written.

    “After I raised serious concerns about Meta’s intends to scrape and abuse creators’ content, I am pleased the firm is finally acknowledging the concerns of publishers and content creators,” Blackburn said in a statement to Nieman Lab on Wednesday. “While this is a step in the right direction, a vague promise to consult with industry stakeholders and potentially delay implementation is not nearly enough. Meta must commit to meaningful changes that protect the intellectual property rights of American creators, and I will continue holding the company accountable until it does.”.

    On October 21, the European Publishers Council signed onto a joint letter to the European Commission, asking the Commission to block the terms from taking effect. The letter claims that Meta’s terms violate the Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

    EPC executive director Angela Mills Wade mentioned on Wednesday that the organization has not heard from Meta about its letter or its concerns.

    “We welcome Meta’s offer to consult publishers fully, and to delay implementation if necessary,” Mills Wade mentioned in an email to Nieman Lab. “However, that consultation must lead to binding contractual safeguards…Using Meta’s services to reach audiences or advertise should not mean granting wider rights to exploit publishers’ journalism, whether collected from websites or uploaded to its platforms. Publishers must retain control over additional uses of their content, including for AI, and the ability to negotiate licenses and payment.”.

    This story has been updated to include a statement from Marsha Blackburn.

    Google Ads AI Max Is Making More Decisions For You – 6 Settings To Audit Now via @sejournal, @brookeosmundson

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google Ads is moving more existing Search campaign functionality into AI Max, giving its automation a larger role in how ads are matched, written, and delivered.
    • Campaigns using automatically created assets and campaign-level broad match settings already began transitioning in September 2026.
    • Sources indicate that google indicates the automatic upgrades are designed to preserve existing campaign settings.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google Ads is moving more existing Search campaign functionality into AI Max, giving its automation a larger role in how ads are matched, written, and delivered.

    Campaigns using automatically created assets and campaign-level broad match settings already began transitioning in September 2026. Dynamic Search Ads will follow in February 2027.

    Sources indicate that google indicates the automatic upgrades are designed to preserve existing campaign settings. However, AI Max also brings additional controls and optimization options that advertisers have the option to enable.

    For PPC managers, this is a good time to review which decisions Google is already making, which settings are active in your accounts, and whether those settings are aligned with your business goals.

    Here’s what to audit before giving AI Max more control over existing Search campaigns.

    Before changing anything, it’s crucial to understand how AI Max is currently configured across your accounts, if at all.

    Recent findings suggest that google’s migration process doesn’t enable every AI Max feature automatically for every campaign. The settings depend on which legacy functionality each campaign was using.

    According to Google’s migration documentation:.

    This is why it’s worth checking each campaign, because two campaigns showing AI Max as enabled may have very different levels of automation running.

    In a recent development, within Google Ads, review the AI Max settings at both the campaign and ad group levels. Specifically, check whether search term matching, text customization, and Final URL expansion are active.

    Search term matching can be controlled at the ad group level, while text customization and Final URL expansion are campaign-level settings.

    I’d also look at whether any campaigns have different configurations than expected, especially those that were recently migrated or created using Google’s default settings.

    The goal here is to establish what’s running before making additional changes. Otherwise, it becomes difficult to evaluate which AI Max features are influencing performance.

    Search term matching is one of the areas I’d spend the most time reviewing, especially in campaigns with tightly defined keyword strategies.

    AI Max can use broad match and keywordless matching technology to identify additional searches based on existing keywords, ads, and landing pages.

    While it can help campaigns reach relevant searches that weren’t covered by the original keyword list, it’s also notorious for introducing traffic that doesn’t fit the campaign’s intended purpose.

    Research from Mike Ryan at Smarter Ecommerce (SMEC) highlights how much AI Max can expand beyond an advertiser’s existing keyword targeting.

    In an analysis of 383 million impressions, Ryan found that more than 25% of impressions attributed to exact match keywords in AI Max-enabled Search campaigns came through AI Max search term matching.

    In a recent development, that doesn’t mean those searches were necessarily irrelevant. However, it does show why advertisers shouldn’t assume exact match keywords are limiting traffic to their original targeting.

    Google’s AI Max reporting documentation outlines additional reporting fields that can help advertisers understand how searches are being matched.

    When reviewing Search terms, I’d focus on:.

    Competitor searches might deserve some extra attention, based on Ryan’s research.

    In SMEC’s research, Ryan documented one account where competitor searches accounted for 69% of total Search impressions.

    That’s a single-account example, but it shows how heavily the traffic mix can lean toward searches outside the advertiser’s original targeting.

    I also wouldn’t judge every new search term solely by whether it converts immediately.

    Some campaigns may have some wiggle room to support earlier-stage research, especially when there’s enough budget to fund it without taking away from stronger existing demand.

    However, if a campaign is already struggling to capture its highest-intent searches, expanding into more informational traffic might be worth excluding for the time being.

    Negative keywords remain available with AI Max, along with brand controls and ad group-level locations of interest.

    Text customization allows Google to generate additional headlines and descriptions using existing ads, keywords, and landing page content.

    For advertisers already using automatically created assets, the audit should focus on what’s being generated and how those assets are performing.

    Google’s optimized asset reporting provides additional performance metrics, including spend and conversions, to help advertisers evaluate the assets being served.

    I’d look closely at three areas:.

    A generated headline could be technically accurate for the business but inappropriate for the campaign’s audience.

    This deserves additional review in industries with legal, compliance, or partner messaging requirements.

    Sources indicate that google allows advertisers to review and remove generated assets. It has also introduced AI Brief and text disclaimer controls to provide additional guidance over generated messaging.

    It has been revealed that see also: Should You Use Auto-Generated Creative? – Ask A PPC.

    There’s another consideration for campaigns that rely on responsive search ad pinning.

    Google’s AI Max documentation confirms that pinning isn’t always respected when Final URL expansion is enabled.

    Sources indicate that when Google selects a different landing page, it may generate ad copy that better matches that destination rather than using the advertiser’s pinned assets. Pinning also isn’t respected when URL inclusions are provided.

    For campaigns with required disclaimers, pricing language, or partner-approved messaging, I’d check whether the current settings support those requirements.

    If pinning is essential, Google recommends avoiding Final URL expansion and URL inclusions.

    When Final URL expansion is enabled, Google can select a different landing page from the advertiser’s website based on the search query.

    That may help when a website has several relevant product or service pages, but it can also create problems when the destination doesn’t align with the campaign’s goals.

    A website might contain informational articles, support documentation, and pages promoting services outside the campaign’s intended focus.

    Those pages could be relevant to someone’s search, but not something worth spending PPC dollars on.

    Google’s landing page and search term reporting can help identify which URLs are receiving traffic through AI Max.

    For lead generation, I’d also look beyond the initial form submission.

    A landing page might generate more leads while attracting more unqualified customers. That can be difficult to identify without qualified lead or sales data.

    Google supports URL exclusions at the campaign level and URL inclusions at the ad group level.

    Those controls can help advertisers limit where traffic goes without necessarily turning off Final URL expansion across an entire campaign.

    For accounts with tightly controlled conversion experiences, I’d review the available URLs before enabling broader expansion.

    See also: Should Your PPC Strategy Focus On The Lead Pipeline Or Revenue?

    Google has reported that advertisers using the full AI Max feature suite see an average of 7% more conversions or conversion value at a similar CPA or ROAS compared with using search term matching alone.

    That figure comes from Google’s internal 2026 data for non-retail advertisers, and it shouldn’t be treated as an expected result for every account.

    Independent research from Smarter Ecommerce offers another perspective.

    In a March 2026 analysis of more than 250 campaigns, Mike Ryan found that AI Max generated a median 13% more conversion value relative to the remaining campaign revenue.

    However, those conversions came at a median CPA that was 16% higher than the campaign baseline.

    Sources indicate that ROAS results also varied considerably. While the median difference was 0%, individual campaign results ranged from 42% above baseline to 35% below it.

    It has been revealed that these figures come from observational campaign data rather than controlled experiments measuring incremental performance. Ryan also noted that the analysis couldn’t account for potential cannibalization across campaigns.

    In a recent development, the research doesn’t mean AI Max is underperforming across the board. It suggests that additional conversion volume may come at a higher cost, with results varying significantly between accounts.

    If broader matching is reaching more informational or earlier-stage searches, those users may need more time before converting. Some may never become customers.

    For lead generation, I’d compare the quality of conversions coming through AI Max against existing traffic. Are those leads qualified? Are they turning into opportunities or customers?

    For ecommerce, revenue, ROAS, margin, and the products being sold can provide more information than conversion volume alone.

    Google has expanded its AI Max experimentation tools, including the ability to maintain brand and location controls during testing.

    For campaigns that haven’t fully adopted AI Max, experiments can help compare performance before enabling additional functionality.

    I’d avoid changing several settings at once because it’s more difficult to attribute performance swings to a particular feature set of AI Max.

    It has been revealed that if the goal is to understand whether broader matching improves performance, structure the test around that decision. The same applies to Final URL expansion or text customization.

    Google’s experiment setup has eligibility restrictions, so not every existing campaign can use the same testing approach.

    For campaigns already migrated with legacy functionality enabled, reviewing current performance may help identify which settings are worth testing next.

    Advertisers still running Dynamic Search Ads have time before Google’s automatic migration begins in February 2027.

    It has been revealed that google says the migration will convert dynamic ad groups into standard ad groups while preserving supported legacy settings and data. Its upgrade documentation also notes that unsupported legacy DSA targets may become read-only.

    I’d review existing dynamic ad targets, URL exclusions, and search term performance before the transition.

    Some campaigns may contain targeting decisions that made sense when they were created but haven’t been revisited recently.

    For advertisers with complex websites or large inventories, confirming which pages and services should remain eligible is worth doing before the migration.

    I wouldn’t approach this audit by immediately turning off AI Max features or adding restrictions across every Search campaign.

    Some accounts may benefit from giving Google more flexibility to find relevant searches, customize messaging, and select landing pages.

    I’d start with campaigns where those decisions could have the greatest impact on performance or where existing controls serve a clear purpose.

    That includes campaigns with limited budgets, strict lead qualification requirements, regulated messaging, or carefully managed landing page experiences.

    For campaigns already performing well, reviewing current settings and reporting may be enough to determine whether additional testing is worthwhile.

    According to recent reports, as Google moves more Search functionality into AI Max, advertisers still have control over several important decisions. Knowing what’s enabled, how Google is using that flexibility, and what results the business is receiving should guide where those controls are applied.

    Recent findings suggest that sometimes, adding just one new ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.11Olives, yecch. And that’s how at least some New York Times readers see its addition of AI features to its popular Cooking app.

    Here’s Genevieve Ko, NYT Cooking senior editor and columnist, explaining the new features:.

    According to recent reports, I naïvely assumed A.I. wouldn’t affect my work as a recipe developer and my role at NYT Cooking, where I oversee the editorial side of our recipes and related stories. But as artificial intelligence improved, our product and engineering colleagues saw its potential to help us create features Cooking users wanted.

    It has been revealed that the Times had previously rolled out AI features aimed at converting volume-based and weight-based measurements (“What’s one cup of bok choy in grams?”) and scaling a recipe up or down to serve more or fewer people. The main fresh feature is focused on ingredient substitutions.

    According to recent reports, say you’re cooking braised white beans and greens with parmesan, NYT Cooking app in hand. But you notice that you’re out of chard and only have spinach. Cooking veterans know that chard is a rough-and-tumble green that has some backbone22There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.”, while spinach is a comparative wimp that will wilt the moment you look at it funny. If you need to sub in spinach for chard, how would the recipe change? Would you, for instance, add the spinach later than you would the chard to account for its pathetic stamina? That’s the sort of thing the upcoming AI feature could account for.

    It has been revealed that cooking staffers “spent countless hours evaluating sample after sample to get the chatbot answers to closely align with how we would answer as culinary experts,” Ko writes. “We applied the same rigor as we do to editing, grounded in Times standards.”.

    But because Ko knows that any AI-powered features are likely to be controversial with a Times audience, she spends quite a lot of space addressing potential objections, everything from “the impact of data centers” to “the concentration of power among A.I. companies” and “the risk of A.I. escaping our control.” These features are designed to enable “the tactile physical pleasure of cooking” and getting a “very real, very human creation” on your table.

    Broadly speaking, commenters weren’t buying it.

    “What a massive disappointment,” wrote Susan from Fresh Jersey. “The internet is full of AI cooking content. I pay you because I prefer mine done by people.”.

    Industry observers note that “This decision misses the mark by such a wide margin it’s baffling,” indicates Ian from Los Angeles. “And the disclosure just as baffling. It would not be inaccurate to summarize the piece as saying ‘I know doing this is bad and I don’t want to be associated with the bad thing so that’s why we are doing the bad thing.'”.

    “Nobody wants this, it’s bad for cooking, it’s bad for the NYT,” writes Bill from Pittsburgh. “Wasting a column trying to gaslight yourself and your audience into believing that it’s anything but is an embarrassment and a waste of everyone’s time.”.

    “PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE DO NOT DO THIS,” says Judah Mann of Latest York. “Oh, wait, you already did. Ok, I’m out.”.

    Or as Naomi from California puts it: “I am sad that AI has breached the one online resource I truly love.”.

    Because I enjoy the irony, I scraped the 171 comments left on the Times’ announcement and asked Codex (running GPT-6.1 Sol, at medium thinking) to do some sentiment analysis. (Twelve of the 171 were comments left by Times staffers; I’m excluding them here.) Roughly 77% of the reader comments were negative about the upcoming AI features, it found, versus 14% positive and the remainder neutral or mixed. Among the biggest categories of complaint: This shouldn’t require AI. AI is destroying the environment. AI is not why I’m paying the Times $390 a year. The adjustments the AI produces are going to be bad.

    Sources indicate that dozens of commenters asked for a way to turn off the feature. “No, not at this time,” Ko responded, “though this feature is completely optional to use.” Indeed: Don’t ask AI to substitute your chard and AI won’t substitute your chard.

    One consistent thread was that cooking is supposed to present you with difficulties and challenges and the whole point is figuring them out by yourself. “Anyone using AI for cooking has no sense of taste and no desire to work out the intricacies of cooking and baking,” writes Michael King from Brooklyn. “To use AI for recipes is beyond the pale. If you are going to use AI, then just cut to the chase and defenestrate yourself.” Or BJ from North Carolina: “So, you’re telling me that I’m too stupid to figure it out on my own?”.

    According to recent reports, meanwhile, the few positive comments tended to focus on how the AI feature had, in fact, made dietary substitutions easier for them. “I love the upcoming AI feature because it quickly (and so far) accurately converts recipes to gluten free,” Anne Wagner from Kansas City writes. “I don’t cook for stress relief,” indicates Andy from San Francisco. “I cook to put dinner on the table. Anything that makes the process a little faster or smoother is welcome.”.

    Industry observers note that about six in 10 Americans said they have at least “some” confidence that news organizations will report the upcoming midterm election results accurately, according to a latest national survey. But only 32% said they had “quite a bit” or “a great deal” of confidence that journalists would do the job.

    In the survey from Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media, 37% said they had either “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” that news outlets would accurately report the election results.

    The survey was completed by a nationally representative sample of 1,057 U.S. adults either online or by telephone earlier this month. The findings echo other national surveys, including a Gallup survey that indicated trust in media to report “fully, accurately, and fairly” at 33% — an increase from an all-time low last year.

    Recent findings suggest that the Medill/Alliance survey found about half of Americans said they had “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” in news outlets to investigate voter fraud claims thoroughly. U.S. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on elections on 70% of days since returning to office — starting with false claims about voter fraud on the first day of his second term.

    According to recent reports, in another bleak result from the same poll, slightly more survey respondents remarked journalists manipulate the news for political or commercial purposes than report it accurately. Across the survey, Democrats reported being more confident in (and trusting of) news organizations than Republicans. Nearly 80% of Republicans said journalists try to manipulate the news compared to 38% of independents and 24% of Democrats.

    More on the survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, here.

    Industry News: Rank Math SEO WordPress Plugin Hit By 16 Vulnerabilities In 2026 via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sixteen vulnerabilities have been discovered in the popular Rank Math SEO plugin in 2026, setting a latest record for vulnerabilities discovered, more than any other SEO plugin.
    • Rank Math’s 2026 vulnerabilities included potential pathways to website takeover, exposure of protected information, and unauthorized changes to WordPress content and data.
    • Although AI is making vulnerability disclosures more common, other SEO plugins like Yoast SEO did not have anywhere near that many vulnerability discoveries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sixteen vulnerabilities have been discovered in the popular Rank Math SEO plugin in 2026, setting a latest record for vulnerabilities discovered, more than any other SEO plugin.

    Rank Math’s 2026 vulnerabilities included potential pathways to website takeover, exposure of protected information, and unauthorized changes to WordPress content and data. All of these things could also have a negative impact on SEO.

    Although AI is making vulnerability disclosures more common, other SEO plugins like Yoast SEO did not have anywhere near that many vulnerability discoveries. The free version of Yoast SEO was reported by Wordfence to have a total of four vulnerabilities in 2026 and only two were discovered in the paid version.

    The sixteen vulnerabilities share certain complications in common but arguably the worst of them are:.

    Remote Code Execution (CVSS rated 8.8) Two vulnerabilities with a CVSS severity score of 8.8 were discovered that could enable attackers with Contributor or Author-level access to execute arbitrary code on the server, potentially leading to complete website compromise.

    Arbitrary File Upload (7.2) One of the vulnerabilities could potentially lead to a website takeover through malicious file uploads, although this vulnerability required Administrator privileges. CVE-2026-104752: Arbitrary File Upload, requiring Administrator-level access or higher. Disclosed October 8, 2026. CVSS 7.2 (High).

    Stored Cross-Site Scripting (7.2) An unauthenticated attacker could potentially execute malicious JavaScript in an Administrator’s browser. Depending on the circumstances, that could lead to privileged actions or account compromise. CVE-2026-66702: Stored Cross-Site Scripting, requiring no authentication. Disclosed July 31, 2026. CVSS 7.2 (High).

    According to recent reports, stored Cross-Site Scripting (7.2) An unauthenticated attacker could potentially execute malicious JavaScript in an Administrator’s browser. Depending on the circumstances, this could enable an attacker to make unauthorized changes to the website or take control of an Administrator’s account. CVE-2026-66702: Stored Cross-Site Scripting, requiring no authentication. Disclosed July 31, 2026. CVSS 7.2 (High).

    It has been revealed that these vulnerabilities could allow attackers to access protected content or sensitive website information without the necessary permissions. Unlike vulnerabilities that enable unauthorized changes, these primarily concern exposing information that should remain restricted, although SQL injection could also allow attackers to manipulate website data.

    Industry observers note that these vulnerabilities could enable attackers to make unauthorized changes to a WordPress website, including modifying content-related data, changing homepage settings, and deleting SEO information. Some could be exploited without logging in, while others required an account but allowed actions beyond that user level’s permissions.

    Recent findings suggest that most vulnerabilities were discovered within a relatively short period. Eleven of the 16 vulnerabilities were discovered between August 27 and October 14, 2026. Of those vulnerabilities, late August and early September saw a concentrated cluster of vulnerability discoveries. Eight were reported between August 27 and September 3, within just eight days.

    It has been revealed that the disclosures continued into October. Five vulnerabilities were reported in October, including three disclosed on October 8 and the latest on October 27.

    In a recent development, as previously stated, Rank Math’s direct competitor, Yoast SEO, only experienced four vulnerabilities during a year which saw an increase in vulnerability discoveries. The unusually high number of vulnerabilities leads to questions about Rank Math’s coding practices, code review, and quality control.

    The other matter in the sixteen vulnerabilities is that are repeated instances of the same kinds of exploits.

    Missing authorization was the most frequently identified vulnerability category. Seven of the 16 entries explicitly mention inadequate permission checks, pointing to recurring problems with enforcing permissions before allowing actions.

    In a recent development, some security problems could lead to complete website compromise. Two vulnerabilities carried CVSS scores of 8.8 and involved remote code execution, allowing attackers who met the required conditions to potentially execute malicious code on the server.

    Overall, the vulnerabilities involved a broad range of security weaknesses. They included unauthorized modifications, information exposure, cross-site scripting, SQL injection, arbitrary file uploads, and remote code execution. The vulnerability discoveries do not point to just one type of coding lapse; they point to a wide range of coding problems.

    The full list of Rank Math vulnerabilities can be found at Wordfence, with links to a description page for each vulnerability.

    • The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try newly introduced things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try newly introduced things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

    Most local newsrooms in the U.S. have one thing in common: They need more money, and many dream of dollars they can use however they want.

    RELATED ARTICLEPress Forward awards $20 million to 205 small local newsroomsSophie CulpepperOctober 16, 2024In 2024, Press Forward, the nonprofit trying to mobilize a philanthropic army for local news, declared it would give at least 100 small local newsrooms — those with annual budgets under $1 million — just that type of unrestricted funding. Almost 1,000 newsrooms applied. Ultimately, Press Forward distributed $20 million to 205 outlets. Most of them received $100,000 each, split over two years.

    Recent findings suggest that I wondered what the recipients had done with the money, and which problems it had (or hadn’t) solved. Between May and October, I spoke or emailed with more than 30 grantees.

    The grantees represented every U.S. state, came from cities, suburbs, and rural areas, and published in multiple languages. They included for-profits and nonprofits, print and digital-only publications, college newsrooms, and public radio stations. Statewide newsrooms with fully staffed teams like The Maine Monitor, scrappy news startups like 285 South, and community newspapers powered by freelancers and part-time staff like the Copper River Record in Alaska all received funding.

    Industry observers note that for many newsrooms, Press Forward was the first grant they’d ever applied for. “Many of the country’s newsrooms are small, and few get foundation grants,” stated Press Forward executive director Dale Anglin. The open call was designed to change that and to distribute the money promptly. Grantees were required to complete two LION sustainability audits a year apart; Press Forward is analyzing that data now and will release its findings next month.1.

    In a recent development, RELATED ARTICLEA study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundationSeth C. LewisOctober 6, 2026“People tell me that what Press Forward did was unusual and rare within philanthropy,” remarked María José Ramírez Braiz, founder and CEO of Midwest-based grantee Te Lo Cuento News.

    “They said to us at the beginning of the grant period, before the shit hit the fan with the federal government, ‘If you need this money to keep the lights on, keep the lights on,'” said Copper River Record editor Allison Sayer, one of the paper’s two part-time staffers. “I feel that this was really a gift.”.

    In a recent development, first-time grant applicants and recipients, in particular, said Press Forward’s recognition gave them credibility and visibility with other funders. And publishers described the funding as a morale boost that validated low-paid work.

    It has been revealed that “It has been a life-changer, a lifesaver for us,” said Gretchen Sporleder Orr, who publishes the World Journal in southern Colorado with her husband. Her voice broke when she talked to me about the funding. “I don’t know if we would be in business right now if it wasn’t for the Press Forward money.”.

    The Real WV “would not still exist without Press Forward,” said Stephen Baldwin, the site’s volunteer publisher. (He’s also the former minority leader for the West Virginia Senate and a pastor of two churches.) The outlet was one of eight grantees that received just two $25,000 grants over two years. “There’s not exactly a lot of capital floating around West Virginia for nonprofit news,” Baldwin said, “and without this outside impact, we wouldn’t be able to do this work.” But he hopes that the site can be less reliant on grants in the future.

    The funding did not save every recipient. One grantee, Atlanta Civic Circle, shut down earlier this year. Atlanta Civic Circle did not receive its second $50,000 grant because it didn’t complete the first LION audit, Anglin mentioned. (Atlanta Civic Circle did not respond to my request for an interview, but executive director Saba Long wrote on LinkedIn in June that “the funding environment for local nonprofit journalism is extraordinarily difficult right now.”) Other recipients have merged or transformed since applying for the grant.2.

    RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026Medill’s annual State of Local News report, released this month, describes a local news ecosystem in a “state of precarity.” That state of precariousness helps explain how $100,000 over two years can be a “godsend,” a “miracle,” and not enough. As one grantee put it, “Right now, these are shanties built on a beach, waiting for a hurricane to come through.”.

    “Press Forward reached newsrooms that don’t have existing relationships with major national funders,” said Nina Ignaczak, the founder, publisher, and editor of Planet Detroit. “The challenge now is whether the commitment holds.”.

    The funding helped newsrooms keep the lights on, whether they used it to pay bills, pay down debt, make payroll, or as a buffer when something went wrong.

    “The flexibility that Press Forward has given us has allowed us to fill — I wouldn’t say emergencies, but unexpected gaps,” said Richard Young, founder and executive director of CivicLex in Kentucky. It brought on a consulting editor to keep city hall coverage going after losing a reporter, and purchased latest software. Without the funding, CivicLex likely would have had to dip into its reserves, he said.

    Bob Bonnar, publisher of the News Letter Journal in Wyoming, used the first payment from Press Forward to upgrade computers and cameras and give some staffers raises. “That chewed up the money very promptly,” he mentioned, “and I probably should have held some of it back because the News Letter Journal ended up having a pretty rough year in 2025.” He had to use about half of the second $50,000 payment to repay an operating loan. The rest covered the remaining revenue shortfall and kept the organization in the black through the winter.

    Vandana Kumar, publisher of the California-based ethnic media outlet India Currents, described the funding as a “stabilizing force” that allowed the newsroom to keep operating despite a contraction in philanthropic giving and cuts to local government advertising.

    The Copper River Record built infrastructure to host digital ads and created a fresh website. It held listening sessions with Native villages in its coverage area and donated subscriptions to local Tribal offices. It improved the design of its print newspaper. Sayer paid freelancers to complete Press Pass training and pursued other professional development. And she was able to take on more ambitious stories about PFAS and “forever chemicals.”.

    According to recent reports, the Press Forward funding was “the biggest single windfall in nearly 20 years for our small community newspaper,” Sandpoint Reader publisher Ben Olson told me. The Idaho-based paper used the money to travel to the state capital for Press Club awards and design a newly introduced media kit, which Olson noted has improved ad sales. The Reader also paid a large chunk of its printing bill, paid its rent a year in advance, and gave staffers bonuses. (The bonuses helped the paper become 100% employee-owned; Olson’s two employees bought in when Olson’s business partner and co-owner retired.).

    The open-ended nature of the grants gave Colorado’s World Journal “the flexibility to be able to make a change, do a thing, and then pivot as needed,” Sporleder Orr said. “When we were in the toilet, all I could think about was, like, ‘Is there going to be anything in the post office today so that I can make payroll?’ ‘Oh, my God, we’ve got to pay rent.’” Sometimes she and her husband skipped their own paychecks to pay staff. The grant gave them “emotional bandwidth” to plan ahead.

    According to recent reports, many grantees used the funding to hire full- or part-time staffers. Sometimes, that worked out well.

    According to recent reports, the Mānoa Mirror, an online newsroom based at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, received two $25,000 grants, which it used to hire a managing editor, a student editorial coordinator, three student reporters, and a social media producer. (The managing editor was paid a stipend, and the other positions were part-time.) The work had previously depended on “faculty goodwill and volunteerism, which was not sustainable for long,” mentioned Hye-ryeon Lee, who was professor and chair of the school of communication and information until retiring this summer. With the new hires, the site went from publishing a few stories a month to publishing daily.

    The Real WV’s first LION audit pointed to a need its small team had already recognized: hiring someone to sell ads. It hired a public school teacher with sales experience (including selling ads for the yearbook) part-time.

    It has been revealed that the funding allowed Te Lo Cuento News to pay contributors consistently and to add contract, part-time positions including a sales manager, an office administrator, and a couple of reporters. The only position it could sustain beyond the grant period is the part-time sales manager, Ramírez Braiz said.

    The Texas Spur is one of five weekly newspapers owned by Paragraph Ranch Media. Originally, the team planned to use the Press Forward grant to secure a loan to improve company housing and hire a journalist based in Spur (population 863 as of 2020). But nobody took the newspaper up on the free housing offer, noted editor and general manager Barbara Brannon. So the company hired four early-career journalists (two full-time, two part-time) living in its 10-county coverage area. Three of the four left for jobs in other industries halfway through their second year. The one who stayed is doing well as a regional sports reporter, Brannon said, and a hire who replaced a person who left is now managing editor for The Post Dispatch.3.

    The turnover Brannon experienced isn’t unique to Spur. Other newsrooms also found hiring with grant money challenging.

    Recent findings suggest that sometimes, that was because of location. “Had we been able to find the right people from the outset, I believe the grant would have had a greater impact on the business,” said Anton Kaufer, regional publisher for Hagadone Media Montana. In rural Northwest Montana, though, recruiting and retaining staff is a challenge, and Hagadone’s Mineral Independent struggled to replace its salesperson and office manager after they retired. The experience “reinforced for us that sustainability isn’t just about having the funding,” Kaufer said. “It’s also about having the people in place to make the most of it.”.

    The World Journal tried placing an ad for a salesperson with the Colorado Press Association and got “absolutely no interest,” Sporleder Orr noted. “People living in northern Colorado don’t particularly want to come live in a teeny-tiny town in a rural, broke part of the state.” (She credited the grant with giving her the mental space to fire a salesperson who wasn’t working out, then regroup.).

    Other times, the money just wasn’t enough. “The reality is that $100,000 over two years isn’t a lot,” one grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. “You can’t hire somebody with that.”.

    EcoRI’s experience illustrates those limitations. Before receiving the Press Forward grant, EcoRI had used other grant funding and reserves to hire a director of development in a one-year contract position. In its grant application to Press Forward, the team proposed converting that role into a full-time staff position with benefits.

    The salary limited the hiring pool, though. The development director position paid $65,000 a year, which “is really not the market rate for a director of development” in the area, publisher and cofounder Jo Detz stated. (She said it should be more like $90,000.) The staffer they ended up hiring came from another state and hadn’t worked in news before. In a staff position, he cost more than he was bringing in. Detz laid him off and eliminated the position last December. She called the experience “heartbreaking.”.

    “At the point where I knew this wasn’t working,” she remarked, “there wasn’t enough runway to pivot, rethink, rehire.”.

    Recent findings suggest that beyond the salary limitations, Detz thinks the development director didn’t have enough runway to succeed. The kind of development the staffer was hired to oversee — major gifts and individual giving — is a long game; “that position would need at least two or three years to begin to see some benefits,” she remarked. Now, she’s back where she started, juggling fundraising with her other work.

    “I know it’s crazy to say that $100,000 over two years wasn’t enough,” she remarked, “but it was not enough to make a meaningful difference to our revenue strategy.”.

    According to recent reports, planet Detroit’s Ignaczak was in a unique position: Around the same time the newsroom received the Press Forward grant, Planet Detroit also received a $500,000 three-year grant from the MacArthur Foundation. That grant allowed her to hire a managing editor, she remarked.

    Ignaczak believes general operating support is what small nonprofit newsrooms need. But to be effective, “I really think fully funding a revenue role for a minimum of three years is what needs to happen to build sustainability, if that is the goal,” she remarked. “And $100,000 over two years is not enough to achieve that.”.

    It has been revealed that notiVisión Georgia, a Spanish-language local news outlet with one full-time staffer, is committed to print in a world moving away from it. The print newspaper is the only way the outlet has been able to use to “generate real economic value,” noted CEO Mónica Pirela, because it’s where local companies want to place ads. The organization spent some of its Press Forward funds on printing and distribution. Pirela wears “every hat” right now, and the organization’s top need is a dedicated sales manager, she said.

    Sources indicate that california’s BenitoLink, meanwhile, used some of the Press Forward funding to begin printing in 2025. That will allow it to apply for newspaper of record status and get paid for running legal notices.

    According to recent reports, in Minnesota, Swift County Monitor-News publisher and owner Reed Anfinson called the grant a “godsend” at a time when tariffs and rising gas prices have driven up printing and delivery costs and weakened advertisers’ budgets. The for-profit Monitor-News put some of its Press Forward funding toward redesigning its print newspaper. Anfinson also purchased materials as part of an “Out of Sight/Out of Mind” advertising campaign stressing the value of print. (He created the campaign himself, using Midjourney for the images.) For news organizations in small towns, Anfinson believes, digital revenue will never be enough to sustain operations.

    Some organizations used the funding to expand their remit beyond news.

    According to recent reports, for instance, the Copper River Record partnered with the Copper River Native Association to include weekly language graphics in the paper for Ahtna, a critically endangered language, coordinating with a local kindergarten class. That project required a lot of time and investment up front, Sayer noted, but it can continue beyond the life of the grant.

    Industry observers note that planet Detroit used some Press Forward funding for reporting, but “the most significant thing the grant made possible wasn’t any single story,” Ignaczak stated. The grant gave the team time to work on its Civic Action Toolbox, which turns reporting into civic engagement prompts. In a story about a local ballot proposal, for instance, the embedded toolbox flags upcoming public meetings, links to contact information for local representatives, and suggests an organization to follow. The tool is also in beta testing with other newsrooms.

    Industry observers note that “The whole project came from having the space to ask what our readers actually need from us beyond information, and then building toward that,” Ignaczak remarked. “Unrestricted funding makes that kind of work possible.”.

    Anfinson of the Monitor-News took the unusual step of writing a grant application on behalf of the local school district, which was losing students to adjacent districts. He used some of the Press Forward funding to match a $2,500 grant to the district. The district then ran $5,000 in ads in a “goodwill effort” to stem declining enrollment. The partnership helped to raise the Monitor-News’s profile, he said, by highlighting the benefits of newspaper advertising.

    Press Forward required grantees to complete two LION sustainability audits. But it also offered optional coaching via the media consulting company Blue Engine to help implement the first audit’s recommendations. Of the 205 grantees, 154 participated in coaching, Anglin said.

    The coaching kicked off in January, with most individual coaches and grantees meeting monthly. Multiple participants remarked the support would have been more beneficial if it were introduced earlier. This was a tradeoff of Press Forward moving quickly to get money out the door, Anglin said.4.

    Sources indicate that this was the first large, unrestricted grant Austin Common had ever received, and it struggled with how to spend the money. “It felt like a lot of pressure,” stated Amy Stansbury, the site’s editor-in-chief and only full-time staffer.

    In a recent development, stansbury wanted to bring on the organization’s first full-time employees, but didn’t want to make those hires (and spend all the grant money) until she had a clear initiative. The coaching helped her figure out which hires made the most strategic sense and how to budget for them.

    A few publishers were lukewarm about the substance of the coaching, but the majority I heard from were enthusiastic. At first, Baldwin was skeptical and worried the coaching might amount to “checking a box.” In practice, though, he noted it’s been “tremendously helpful” for tasks like writing the job description for the Real WV’s sales position.

    Sources indicate that sporleder Orr called the coaching “incredible.” The monthly sessions helped her with everything from tackling grant proposals to improving her Google Analytics skills. The combination of money and coaching, she added, “makes sure that the recipients don’t just continue doing business as usual.”.

    In a recent development, in addition to the funding, Press Forward paid for grantees to attend conferences. Anglin mentioned 111 grantees attended the Lenfest News Philanthropy Summit in Philadelphia in 2025, 81 attended the same conference (which I also attended) in 2026, and 87 attended the Business of Local conference in Salt Lake City in 2025. A handful of grantees attended affinity conferences.

    Stansbury found attending conferences for the first time helpful and eye-opening. It taught her “there’s this secret shadow world of [invitation-only] foundation and grant funding.” Press Forward’s travel support to attend a national conference was “transformative” for India Currents, Kumar said, giving it visibility and access to relationship-building.

    Industry observers note that to small newsrooms, the grant felt like a Press Forward stamp of approval that put them on the map for other funders. The Mirror’s Lee called the Press Forward funding “instrumental” in securing a $20,000 grant from a local foundation. But that was an exception among publishers I heard from; most didn’t feel the visibility and credibility conferred by the grant directly translated to other funders giving them more money.

    So several publishers, including Ramírez Braiz of Te Lo Cuento News, would like to see Press Forward go a step further and make individual introductions to funders. “Those more personal introductions can make a major difference for small organizations,” she mentioned.

    Ramírez Braiz also called for “more shared learning around outcomes and impact.” Few grantees had a good sense of what others in the cohort were up to, and some were interested in more knowledge sharing with peer organizations, though the day-to-day grind of keeping one’s own newsroom running was a common impediment.

    Since 2023, Anglin said, Press Forward’s network of more than 130 funders has invested $258 million directly in newsrooms. That suggests that over half of the more than $400 million the coalition indicates it’s invested has gone to newsrooms.

    Industry observers note that when Press Forward first declared the direct funding for newsrooms, it “felt really awesome,” the grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. To the grantee, it was meaningful to see Press Forward give funding to more organizations than planned in response to the scale of need. But when Press Forward went on to a second funding round in which single organizations, including both newsrooms and newsroom-adjacent organizations like the International Women’s Media Foundation and LION, received as much as $1.5 million for infrastructure projects, the same grantee mentioned it felt like “a slap in the face.”.

    It has been revealed that “Many of the problems newsrooms face aren’t unique to them individually,” Anglin stated. “If we are attempting to solve problems at scale, we have to intervene not just at the newsroom level, but at the systems level, too.” She said that because many of the infrastructure grantees serve multiple newsrooms, “investing in them creates a multiplier effect across the industry.”.

    Industry observers note that the argument that funding support organizations and infrastructure lifts more boats is “a cop-out,” this publisher said. “I think the philanthropists know it, I think the associations know it, and I think the potential grantees that are not funders or associations or intermediaries know it.”.

    According to recent reports, young had a different perspective. Because of CivicLex’s broad scope, it seeks out funding from both democracy funders and journalism funders. Young thinks local news funders are way ahead on getting dollars into local communities.

    Recent findings suggest that “I think Press Forward has done one of the more effective jobs of anything I’ve seen in the broader landscape of my world, and the civic renewal space, of delivering resources to the local level,” he said. (He added, “No one is ever happy in the local news ecosystem when I say that folks in the local news ecosystem don’t know how good they have it. That does not win me a lot of friends.”).

    Most publishers I heard from see grants like this as critical to continued operation, yet they’re wary of overreliance on philanthropy.

    Sources indicate that young noted he’d be surprised if local news is still a focus for national philanthropy in eight years. “Filling your cup up with money that will be impossible to recover in four years is a danger zone,” he added.

    Right now, more than 80% of Planet Detroit’s revenue mix comes from foundations. Ignaczak said the organization hopes to bring that down to 50% by 2028. “But for nonprofit newsrooms covering environmental and public health problems in a mid-size metro, general operating grants aren’t a crutch,” she said. “They’re infrastructure.”.

    As for Press Forward, “Time will tell, as these grants go away, what impact [they’ve] actually had on the newsrooms that received [them], how many have managed to build sustainability,” she added. “I think a newsroom that needed $50,000 to survive to next year had problems that $50,000 isn’t going to solve.”.

    LOOKOUT executive director Jake Hylton believes there’s enough funding to go around. “While there may not be enough to support every single newsroom at a very large amount,” he noted, “I do believe that there is a larger investment in news that could be done.”.

    A second grantee who asked to stay anonymous was blunt about their fears for the future. “We’re scared shitless about 2027,” this person mentioned, “because not only is the Press Forward money not returning, we also see none of the national grants that sustained us in 2024 and previous years.”.

    Sources indicate that the Copper River Record was in the black before receiving this grant, and the lean paper’s fixed overhead remains low. For the Record, Press Forward has been like “a fairy godmother,” Sayer noted.

    In a recent development, “I’m not going to lie: I will miss having the money to say yes to any reasonable story,” she continued. “But I think that, even going back to our original budget, the strength of what we learned will continue to help us deliver a higher quality paper that is more relevant to the communities we serve.”.

    In a recent development, the Sandpoint Reader, Olson said, is “surviving” right now. “We’d love to be thriving,” he added, “but we’re happy to continue to survive when many print publications aren’t.” He credited the Press Forward grant with giving the burned-out team “the chance to fall in love with our industry again.”.

    Sporleder Orr feels nervous about what’s ahead, but with the World Journal in a much more comfortable cash flow position, she and her husband are “in a way better mental state about the business.”.

    Sources indicate that “We feel good about the future right now, that we are going to be able to keep going and make it,” she stated. “We’re back to, ‘This is what we do ’til we die.'”.

    Information Security Engineer - Application Security at Camunda

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes.
    • We're hiring an Information Security Engineer with a focus on Application Security to join our Information Security team at Camunda.
    • Sources indicate that we are a team that takes security seriously without making it feel like a locked door.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale. Trusted by over 700 organizations worldwide, including 9 of top 10 US banks, Camunda helps enterprises boost operational efficiency, accelerate time-to-value, and deliver better customer experiences.Fully remote and global, we are in the middle of something bigger: transforming into an AI-first organisation, built on our own platform. We use Agentic AI to automate, orchestrate intelligent processes, and elevate human contribution across every team.Named GP Bullhound’s Top 100 Next Unicorn list, 2025 Great Place to Work certified. Visionary in 2025 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies. ranked 3rd in Flexa's 2026 Most Flexible Companies, We’re growing fast and looking for top talent to join our team. If you want meaningful work, visible impact and put something genuinely rare on your CV, keep reading.

    Hi there! We're hiring an Information Security Engineer with a focus on Application Security to join our Information Security team at Camunda.

    Sources indicate that we are a team that takes security seriously without making it feel like a locked door. We work in a transparent, straightforward way, and we care about doing the work right rather than just checking a compliance box.

    Recent findings suggest that you will work side by side with our R&D engineers: reviewing designs, threat modeling fresh features, digging into code and helping teams make good, risk-based decisions about the vulnerabilities that come in. You'll also help build the internal tools that make this work scale, including our CVE registry and the LLM-assisted workflows we use to analyse code and triage findings.

    Recent findings suggest that camunda is an AI-first organization, and InfoSec is no exception: AI agents are part of how we review code, assess vulnerabilities, and build our tools. You will help shape how that works.

    Recent findings suggest that this is a hands-on role for someone who already has solid AppSec foundations and wants to grow. We are a generalist team, so you will also take part in our on-call rotation and incident response, and get exposure to other areas of security. But most of your time will be spent with engineers and building and maintaining internal tools and processes.

    Vulnerability management: triage findings from SCA, container and code scanning, external reports and internal security testing; assess whether Camunda is actually affected; agree fix / mitigate / accept with engineering and follow through to release.

    Threat modeling and security reviews: run threat modeling sessions and design reviews with R&D teams for fresh features and architecture changes, and turn the results into concrete, prioritised actions.

    Code analysis with LLMs: use and improve LLM-assisted tooling (agents, prompts, reusable skills) to review code, validate findings and reproduce challenges, while applying your own judgement to know when the model is wrong.

    It has been revealed that build internal security tooling: contribute to the CVE registry and related automation that connects scanners, engineering teams, and customer communication. Much of it is built on Camunda itself.

    Help engineers do the secure thing by default: answer questions, review pull requests, improve guidelines and occasionally run a session or workshop.

    On-call and incident response: share the InfoSec on-call rotation with the other engineers and help investigate and resolve security incidents.

    Support the wider team: help write security advisories for our customers, answer customer security questions and support audits.

    What You Will Bring to the Role.

    Around 3+ years in security or software engineering, with at least 2 of them working on application or product security (AppSec, product security, pentesting, or a security-focused developer role all count).

    Experience at a SaaS or software product organization, working closely with engineering teams that ship often through modern CI/CD and cloud environments.

    Hands-on vulnerability triage: you've worked with tools like Snyk, Trivy, Semgrep, CodeQL or similar, can tell a real issue from a false positive, and can explain how exploitable something actually is in context (CVSS, exploitability, configuration).

    According to recent reports, threat modeling and design review experience (e.g. STRIDE) on real systems, ideally web apps, APIs, or distributed services.

    You read and write code. You're comfortable reading Java (Camunda is built on it) well enough to follow a data flow and spot a security bug. You can write scripts and small tools and contribute to an existing codebase with review.

    It has been revealed that you build with AI, not just chat with it. You use AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot or similar) in your daily work to write tools, analyse code or automate tasks. And you know their output still needs a second look, especially when it comes to security.

    Sources indicate that clear, friendly communication with engineers. You see yourself as an enabler, not a gatekeeper, and you can explain risk to people who aren't security specialists.

    Some Python and/or JavaScript experience, or experience building internal tools.

    Willingness to learn and use Camunda, since we build a lot of our own security automation on it. Prior BPMN / workflow experience is a plus.

    Experience responding to security incidents or being part of an on-call rotation.

    Exposure to security advisories, CVE disclosure or bug bounty programmes.

    Knowledge of AI/LLM security risks (OWASP Top 10 for LLMs / agentic apps, prompt injection, tool abuse).

    Experience securing Kubernetes or container-based workloads, or open-source / B2B software.

    This role is an existing vacancy.

    It has been revealed that we offer competitive, fair, and transparent compensation. Salary ranges are location-based, with Standard and Major markets (global tech hubs) reflecting local competition.

    In a recent development, the Annual Total Target Cash (base salary + 100% variable target, where applicable) shown below spans from the minimum in a Standard market to the maximum in a Major market. Final offers depend on skills, experience, and location, and we typically hire in the first half of the range to allow room for growth:.

    United States: $119,900.00 to $193,200.00.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • AI is changing how customers discover and evaluate brands.
    • Enterprises need to think beyond rich results and develop the business context they publish for machines.
    • In 2027, schema markup has to be upgraded in order to maintain visibility in AI SERPs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    AI is changing how customers discover and evaluate brands.

    Enterprises need to think beyond rich results and develop the business context they publish for machines.

    In 2027, schema markup has to be upgraded in order to maintain visibility in AI SERPs.

    Get a free, personalized AI-Ready Schema Markup Scorecard, Now →.

    According to recent reports, the latest job I see for schema markup is to help AI understand your business, not just make individual pages eligible for rich results. That means explicitly describing your products, services, people, and locations, showing how they connect, and keeping those facts and relationships accurate as your business changes.

    One of the biggest questions I hear from enterprise marketing leaders today is: How do we make sure AI is getting our brand right? It’s a fair question.

    AI is increasingly influencing how customers discover, research, and choose businesses. Unlike traditional search, where customers could visit your website and form their own understanding, AI now brings information together from across the web to create answers on their behalf.

    Industry observers note that that information might come from your website, a third-party directory, customer reviews, or an article published years ago. And not all of it is necessarily accurate, complete, or up to date.

    Here’s what I think is important for marketers to recognize: You can’t control everything AI indicates about your business. But you can take greater control of the information you give it, and that starts with your website.

    Your website is one of the most valuable sources of information you own. It’s where you define who you are, what you offer, the expertise you bring to market, and what you want your business to be known for.

    This is why I believe preparing the information you own for AI is one of the most important investments enterprise marketers can make today.

    And if your organization already has schema markup, you’ve already started building that foundation. The opportunity now is to think bigger about what it can do, and make sure your strategy is built for the job schema markup needs to do today and tomorrow, not just the one it did yesterday.

    Industry observers note that the good news is that if you’ve already invested in schema markup, you’re not starting from scratch. But not all schema markup is created equal. Before you focus on doing more, ask whether what you already have gives machines a clear, connected understanding of your business.

    The opportunity is to assess the foundation you’ve built, identify where it could be stronger, and build from there.

    Here are three questions I’d encourage enterprise marketing leaders to ask.

    Pro Tip: Use a AI-Ready Schema Markup Scorecard to assess your current foundation and identify opportunities to strengthen how machines understand your business.

    Industry observers note that having schema markup across your website is a great start. But is it capturing the information that actually matters to your business?

    Think about your most notable products, services, locations, and areas of expertise. Does your markup describe them accurately and in enough detail? Or is it simply meeting the minimum requirements for a search feature? The goal isn’t just more schema markup; it’s more meaningful markup.

    Industry observers note that it’s one thing for machines to recognize the individual parts of your business. It’s another for them to understand how everything fits together. Are your people, products, services, and locations consistently identified and connected? Can machines recognize when different pages are talking about the same thing?

    In a recent development, think about a healthcare system. It might have schema markup describing its physicians, hospitals, and medical services. That’s a great start. But does that information clearly communicate which physicians specialize in which treatments? Where they practice? Which services are available at each location? And how all of those things connect back to the healthcare system?

    Move beyond describing individual pages to communicating a connected picture of your business.

    In a recent development, your business is constantly evolving. Latest services, new locations, new expertise. And as your website content changes, your schema markup needs to keep up. Because it’s not enough for your website to tell one story to customers while your structured data tells another to machines.

    As your website evolves, does your schema markup keep pace, reflecting the same accurate information and maintaining the relationships that connect your business?

    In a recent development, our Wells Fargo case study illustrates why this matters. Wells Fargo encountered an AI Overview that incorrectly identified a branch as permanently closed. By strengthening the structured information on its website, the team helped address that inaccurate answer.

    In a recent development, you can’t control every answer AI generates. But you can take greater control of the accuracy and consistency of the information you’re giving it to work with. And that requires governance to be part of your approach from the beginning.

    We need to think differently about what we’re asking our schema markup to accomplish. We should question whether we’re giving machines the information and context they need to understand our business as a whole, and recognize our relevance to the topics that matter most.

    But here’s the challenge: Across large enterprise websites, that information is often spread across thousands of pages, managed by different teams, and constantly changing. Even when the information is accurate on individual pages, it doesn’t always tell a clear, connected story about the business.

    And sometimes, we’re contributing to the confusion ourselves. As Schema App’s CTO Mark van Berkel discusses in Forbes, AI doesn’t always need to hallucinate incorrect information. Sometimes, it works with conflicting information businesses have already published.

    If we want AI to understand our business, we need to give it more than individual pieces of information. We need to help it understand how those pieces fit together. And for large enterprises, that’s not a small challenge.

    It has been revealed that think about everything your organization publishes across its website. Your products and services, locations, your people and their expertise, the topics you want to be known for. All of that information helps tell the story of your business. But across thousands of pages, different teams, and constantly changing content, those connections aren’t always clear.

    What if we started thinking about our website not just as a collection of pages, but as a connected source of truth about our business? That’s the opportunity I see with a Marketing Context Layer.

    According to recent reports, A Marketing Context Layer is a governed foundation of information about your business that helps machines understand who you are, what you offer, what you’re known for, and how it all connects. It starts with the information you own and publish on your website.

    Through advanced schema markup, you can make important business facts and relationships explicit, connecting them into a Content Knowledge Graph that can be maintained as your business evolves.

    According to recent reports, and this isn’t just a marketing conversation. Forrester has been exploring the importance of context layers in enterprise AI, recognizing the role of connected business knowledge in helping AI systems interpret and use information. I believe there’s an notable opportunity to apply that same thinking to marketing. If enterprises are investing in governed business context to power AI internally, shouldn’t we also be thinking about the context we’re publishing for AI to understand us externally?

    It has been revealed that this is where schema markup becomes much more than an SEO tactic. It’s the starting point for building a connected, governed foundation of information about your business. One you can keep improving, maintaining, and putting to work as search and AI experiences evolve.

    As our CTO, Mark van Berkel, explores in Forbes, the organizations that want to make meaningful use of AI need to invest in the information foundations that support it.

    I believe we’re at an exciting turning point for enterprise marketers. We’ve spent years investing in our websites, creating content, and building our presence in search. Now we have an opportunity to make those investments work harder by helping machines understand the business behind the content.

    And as AI continues to evolve, from search and answers to emerging agentic experiences, having clear, connected, and reliable business information will only become more crucial.

    Industry observers note that because the goal isn’t just to be found. It’s to be understood. And that starts with taking ownership of the information we control.

    You may already have schema markup. But how well is it communicating the full story of your business?
